result:
`final.py` scores **86.1** on the search split (reference 1.351 s vs. 0.0157 s CPU), using **6 of the 24** scorer calls. The scorer found no missing, extra or repeated pairs.

**How it works:** it's the standard "prefix filtering" method for finding similar sets.
- **Exact duplicates first.** Records with the same word set are grouped up front, and all pairs within each group are reported directly.
- **Small sets skip the search.** Under the ≥80% rule, a set of 3 or fewer words can only match an identical set, so after grouping those need no further work. A 4-word set is indexed but never searched from, since it can only match a 5-word superset.
- **Prefix filtering for the rest.** Words get one fixed order across all records, with rare words first. Records are processed from smallest to largest. Each record looks up only its first `a − ⌈4a/5⌉ + 1` words (`a` is its word count) and adds only its first `a − ⌈8a/9⌉ + 1` words to the index. Two records that are 80% alike are guaranteed to share a word in those short prefixes.
- **Size filter.** Each index list keeps a moving start pointer that skips records too small to reach 80% (`5|B| < 4|A|`).
- **Exact check.** Every candidate is confirmed with the same integer test as the spec, `9·|A∩B| ≥ 4·(|A|+|B|)`.
- **Cheap word order.** Instead of counting how often each word appears, words are ranked in reverse order of their first appearance, which is all done in C. Common words show up early, so they land at the back of each prefix. On my category-sorted test data, this was faster than both exact counting and a sampled-count version.

**Version history (search score):**

| Version | Change | Score |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Prefix filtering | 67.6 |
| 3 | Imported a private `collections` helper | rejected by the scorer's file check |
| 4 | Plain dict counting, small sets skipped | 80.6 |
| 6 | Bulk set building and duplicate grouping, first-appearance word order | 87.0 |
| 11 / final | One index pass, small fast path | 87.1 / 86.1 |

The gap between 87.1 and 86.1 is run-to-run noise; local timings of those versions were the same within noise. Most of the time now goes to splitting the records and ranking the words, and very few pairs get checked in full, so I stopped tuning there.

**Checks:** besides the scorer, `final.py` matched the reference on 1,500 random small tests and a few hand-written edge cases. These covered tabs, newlines, Unicode spaces, case differences, empty records and repeated words. It also matched on three generated catalogue-style datasets, one of them sorted by category so that common words first appear late.

`final.py` uses the standard library only (`itertools.chain`). My scratch files (the `c*.py` versions, generators and benchmarks) are left in the same folder.
